operations.evidence: Force Name identifies the police force area in which an offence was recorded; the recorded force area will generally be the same area where the offence took place
generally does not mean always; recording area must not be treated as an exact incident coordinate
CSP Name identifies the Community Safety Partnership area in which offences were recorded; a CSP generally corresponds to single or combined local-authority boundaries
CSP boundaries are not parcel boundaries; combined-authority cases require the geographic reference table
the geographic reference table maps each CSP to its police force area; the mapping is edition-specific reference data
mapping must be versioned with the release; names alone are not a stable join key
the geographic reference table maps CSP and police-force areas to regions; region is a separate field from force and CSP
region aggregation must not replace lower-level geography; boundary changes require reference-table checks
the geographic reference table includes an ONS Code for each CSP; the code is described as a unique CSP identifier
the code must be joined through the matching release; an ONS code is not a parcel or police-neighbourhood identifier
figures are provided at Police Force Area and Community Safety Partnership levels; the two products support different geographic analyses
PFA and CSP rows must not be mixed without explicit aggregation; neither level supplies parcel observations
users may need to filter across multiple columns; different years can require searching across multiple sheets
single-sheet extraction can omit periods; filters must retain force CSP offence and period fields
the guide states that figures in the tables are additive; quarterly offence figures can be aggregated when dimensions match
addition is valid only for non-overlapping periods and matching geography/offence definitions; rates and percentages are not additive
all four quarters of a 12-month financial period can be summed for a PFA; the aggregation uses the Financial Year and Financial Quarter fields
revised quarter editions must be consistent; rolling-12-month and financial-year totals must not be conflated
CSP-level totals do not necessarily equal national police-recorded-crime totals; scope differences are an official caveat
a CSP sum must not be labelled as the national total without reconciliation; scope exclusions must remain explicit
British Transport Police data are excluded from CSP-level data; this exclusion contributes to differences from national totals
BTP incidents must not be silently assigned to territorial CSPs; PFA and CSP scope must be compared before aggregation
PFA crime rates can be calculated with ONS population estimates; the numerator comes from police-recorded-crime counts
population edition and geography must match the crime period; rates are not direct measures of victimisation risk
CSP crime rates can be calculated with ONS local-authority population estimates; the CSP geography generally follows local-authority boundaries
combined or non-coterminous CSPs require denominator reconciliation; population denominators are not parcel counts
crime rates are typically expressed per 1,000 population; the convention is used because many crime types have low volumes
the denominator convention must be displayed; different rate bases must not be compared without conversion
the guide defines rate calculation as crimes divided by population multiplied by 1,000; the formula applies to matching area and period
zero or missing denominators must fail closed; counts and rates must be stored as different measures
ONS publishes rates for main crime types at CSP level; the official rate tables can be used instead of recomputing where available
published rates retain ONS definitions and revisions; main crime types do not cover every offence code
PFA-level rates are available in ONS table P1; the table belongs to the Police Force Area data-table release
table edition must match the crime period; PFA rates are not CSP or parcel rates
quarterly police-recorded-crime figures are revised every quarter; revisions reflect the live administrative nature of the data
quarterly values require edition metadata; a revised quarter must replace rather than duplicate its predecessor
a recorded crime can later be deleted when transferred to another PFA; the deletion changes previously supplied quarterly figures
transfer deletion is not evidence that no incident occurred; origin and destination records must not be double counted
a recorded crime can later be deleted when it is cancelled; cancellation contributes to quarterly revisions
cancellation categories require official reason metadata; deleted records must not be retained as current offences
some quarterly cells before 2019 can contain negative numbers; the values arise from the historical return mechanism
negative values are not impossible crime counts to be clipped to zero; the period and return method must be retained
before 2019 forces could deduct transferred or cancelled crimes from cumulative monthly returns; the deduction could create a negative value within a quarter
the mechanism must not be interpreted as negative incidents; historical aggregation requires the full financial-year context
the historical deduction system was designed to keep financial-year figures accurate; it also reduced resubmission burden on forces
quarterly volatility can remain even when annual totals reconcile; the rationale does not remove other data-quality limitations
Making off without payment code 49A was introduced separately in April 2013; the classification boundary is explicitly documented
pre- and post-introduction coding must be versioned; the code change is not an incident trend by itself
before April 2013 making off without payment was included within code 53B; the later separate code changes category composition
53B before 2013 is not directly identical to 53B afterward; historical extraction must use the reference table
a back series for offence 49A is provided for 2002/03 to 2012/13; the back series supports a more consistent time series
back-series values are reconstructed rather than uniformly contemporaneous; series provenance must remain visible
the 49A back series mixes actual force data and estimated data; the guide explicitly discloses this mixed provenance
actual and estimated components must not be treated as equally observed; confidence and provenance fields are required
a new burglary classification was introduced from April 2017; the change replaced earlier domestic and non-domestic categories
classification change can create discontinuity; old and new categories require mapping rather than simple renaming
residential and non-residential burglary became the principal subcategories from April 2017; they replaced domestic and non-domestic burglary respectively
the terms are not guaranteed to have identical boundaries; comparisons require the official classification notes
residential burglary includes buildings or parts of buildings within or forming part of a dwelling boundary; the definition extends beyond the main occupied structure
the statistical definition is not a cadastral parcel rule; building-context data are required for local interpretation
from April 2023 residential burglary was split into home and unconnected-buildings subcategories; the change adds detail within residential burglary
pre-2023 series lacks the same split; new subcategories must not be backfilled without official data
